problemStatement:
Industrial line shafts and belt-driven shaft systems are used to distribute rotational power from a common drive to multiple machines or auxiliary components. Pulleys mounted along the shaft transfer power through belts, while bearings support and align the rotating shaft. Similar arrangements are found in machine shops, conveyors, packaging systems, process equipment, and older centralized power-transmission systems.

Although the shaft's main purpose is to transmit torque, the belts also apply transverse forces to the pulleys. These forces are transferred into the shaft and then into the bearings, producing vertical shear force and bending moment along the shaft. The magnitude of the bending depends on both the pulley-force resultants and their locations relative to the bearings. A pulley mounted outside a bearing creates an overhung load, which can significantly increase bending demand in the adjacent shaft region.

Before selecting a shaft diameter or performing a later bending-stress or fatigue calculation, engineers first determine the bearing reactions and construct the complete shear-force and bending-moment diagrams. These diagrams reveal where the shaft experiences its largest bending moment and therefore identify the shaft station that should be examined first in a subsequent strength analysis. The present problem isolates this transverse-bending behavior; torsional power transmission is part of the industrial context but is not included in the assigned calculations.
engineeringGoal: Determine the vertical bearing reactions, construct the shear-force and bending-moment diagrams for the shaft, and identify the location and magnitude of the absolute maximum bending moment.
